t.4.8.1: Delighted by those words, the monkey Sugrīva spoke these words to Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.8.2: Without doubt I am in every way favoured by the gods, I whose friend you are, you who are endowed with excellent virtues.
t.4.8.3: O sinless Rāma, with you as my ally it would surely be possible to win even the kingdom of the gods; how much more, then, my own kingdom, O lord!
t.4.8.4: Thus I, O Rāghava, am worthy of honour among my kinsmen and friends, since I have gained, with fire as witness, a friend born of the Rāghava lineage.
t.4.8.5: I too am a fitting friend for you, as you will come to know in time; but I am not able to speak myself of the virtues that reside in me.
t.4.8.6: But for the most part, the affection of great-souled men like you, whose selves are perfected, remains unwavering, just as the steadfastness of the self-possessed does.
t.4.8.7: Silver or gold, garments or ornaments: the good regard these as undivided, held in common among good people.
t.4.8.8: Whether rich or poor, whether suffering or happy, whether faultless or with faults, a friend is the highest refuge.
t.4.8.9: Seeing affection of such a kind, people proceed to give up wealth, to give up comfort, or even to give up the body itself for the sake of a friend.
t.4.8.11: Then, seeing Rāma standing there along with the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva cast his restless eyes all around the forest.
t.4.8.10: Rāma said “So be it” to the sweet-spoken Sugrīva in the presence of the wise Lakṣmaṇa, as if before the splendour of wise Vāsava himself.
t.4.8.12: Then the lord of the monkeys saw, not far away, a sāla tree in full bloom, lightly covered with leaves and adorned by bees.
t.4.8.13: Breaking off a single branch of that sāla tree, thick with leaves and full of blossoms, Sugrīva spread it out and sat down together with Rāghava.
t.4.8.14: Then, seeing those two seated, Hanūmān too tore off a branch of a sāla tree and seated the modest Lakṣmaṇa upon it.
t.4.8.15: Then the delighted Sugrīva, out of affection, spoke gently to Rāma in a sweet voice, his syllables faltering with joy.
t.4.8.16: Wronged by my brother, I wander here on Ṛśyamūka, the finest of mountains, tormented by fear, deeply afflicted, my wife carried off.
t.4.8.17: Thus I live terrified, sunk in fear, my mind bewildered, wronged by my brother Vālin, who has made me his enemy, O Rāghava.
t.4.8.19: Thus addressed, the radiant Kākutstha, knower of dharma and devoted to dharma, replied to Sugrīva as if smiling.
t.4.8.18: O you who strike fear into all the worlds, I am tormented by fear of Vālin and have no protector; you should show your grace to me as well.
t.4.8.20: Help bearing fruit is the mark of a friend, and harm is the mark of an enemy. This very day I shall slay him who carried off your wife.
t.4.8.21: For these arrows of mine, feathered, of great speed and fierce brilliance, adorned with gold, have sprung from the reed forest of Kārttikeya.
t.4.8.22: Fletched with heron feathers, like the thunderbolt of great Indra, well-jointed and keen-tipped, they are like enraged serpents.
t.4.8.23: Behold Vālin, your enemy who is a brother in name only, the doer of wrongs, struck down by my arrows and lying shattered like a mountain.
t.4.8.24: Hearing the words of Rāghava, Sugrīva, lord of the army, attained incomparable joy and said, "Excellent, excellent!"
t.4.8.25: O Rāma, I am overwhelmed by grief, and you are the refuge of those afflicted by sorrow. Regarding you as my friend, I pour out my lament before you.
t.4.8.26: For by the giving of your hand, with Agni as witness, you have been made my friend, more dear to me than my very life; this I swear to you by truth itself.
t.4.8.28: Having spoken these words, his eyes clouded with tears, he could not speak aloud, his voice choked by tears.
t.4.8.27: Regarding you as a friend, I speak to you in full trust: there is a sorrow hidden deep within me that constantly burns my mind.
t.4.8.29: But Sugrīva, in Rāma's presence, steadfastly held back the rush of tears that had come upon him suddenly, like the surge of a river.
t.4.8.30: But the splendid one, restraining those tears, wiping his fair eyes and sighing deeply, spoke again to Rāghava.
t.4.8.31: Formerly, O Rāma, I was cast down from my own kingdom by Vālin; and after making me hear harsh words, the stronger one drove me out.
t.4.8.32: My wife, dearer to me even than my life, was carried off by him, and those who were my friends have been bound in fetters.
t.4.8.34: Because of this very suspicion, O Rāghava, even on seeing you I did not approach, being afraid; for in the presence of danger all beings are afraid.
t.4.8.33: And that utterly wicked-souled one strives for my destruction, O Rāghava; many times the monkeys sent by him for that purpose have been slain by me.
t.4.8.35: Only these companions of mine, with Hanumān at their head, remain to me; therefore, though I have fallen into distress, I still sustain my life today.
t.4.8.36: For these devoted monkeys guard me on every side; they always go with me when I must go, and they stay when I stay.
t.4.8.37: This, O Rāma, is my story in brief, for what would be gained by telling it to you at length? My enemy is my elder brother, Vālī, whose prowess is renowned.
t.4.8.38: For with his destruction my sorrow would at once be gone; my happiness and my very life depend upon his destruction.
t.4.8.40: Having heard these words, Rāma said this to Sugrīva: "For what reason did the enmity arise? I wish to hear it truly."
t.4.8.39: O Rāma, I, stricken with grief, have made known to you this, the end of my sorrow. Whether he is in distress or free from distress, a friend is always the refuge of his friend.
t.4.8.42: Indeed, having heard that you have been humiliated, my mighty anger swells, shaking my heart, like the rushing force of waters in the rainy season.
t.4.8.41: Having heard the cause of your enmity, O monkey, I shall readily arrange what is to be done next, after weighing the strength and weakness of both sides.
t.4.8.43: Speak joyfully and with confidence: even as the bow is being strung, the arrow is already loosed by me and your enemy is struck down.
t.4.8.44: Thus addressed by the great-souled Kākutstha, Sugrīva, together with his four vānaras, attained incomparable joy.
t.4.8.45: Then Sugrīva, his face beaming with joy, began to tell the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa the true cause of the enmity.
